title: Duet
summary: Play the piece with a family member, or with a recording of yourself, and lock your beat to theirs.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil
a family member to play or sing with, or a second phone with a recording of yourself
tone generator app on the phone (free)

figure.alt: A bar of four steady clicks, standing for the one shared beat both players lock to, so that playing together, neither part quietly speeds up or slows down on its own.

steps.title: Duet
steps.body:
Playing alone, only your own sense of time matters. Playing with someone else, or with your own recording, means matching a beat that is not fully under your control. That is a different skill from playing well by yourself.

1. Play the piece once alone at your usual tempo, and note the metronome number.
2. Record that run-through if you will duet with your own recording, or ask a family member to play or sing alongside you.
3. Play together, listening for whether you speed up or slow down to match the other part.
4. Fix any spot where you pulled away from the other sound, practising it slowly, then together again.

Ensemble playing is its own skill, separate from playing alone well, and it only grows by actually playing with another sound in the room.

figure.alt: A bar of eight beats with a pulse on the first and the fifth. This stands for the slow wobble, called a beat, heard when two notes that are almost but not quite the same pitch, 440 and 444 wiggles a second, drift in and out of step.

steps.title: Beats between close notes
steps.body:
Two notes that are almost, but not quite, the same pitch do not blend cleanly. They wobble, getting louder and softer in a slow pulse called a beat. The number of beats each second equals the difference between the two wiggle rates.

Predict first: if one tone wiggles 440 times a second and another wiggles 444, how many beats will you hear each second? Write your number in the Practice log.

Measure: open a tone generator app, set one tone to 440 and another to about 444, then play them together. Count the wobbles over ten seconds, then divide by ten.

Compare: how close was your count to your prediction?

Teach it: explain why two instruments that are almost, but not quite, in tune sound wobbly together. A tuner is happy only when the beats disappear.

figure.alt: A bar of four steady clicks, the shared beat both players play against, noted at the start of the sitting and checked again once the parts are played together.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: play alone once, note the tempo, then record or set up the duet
Sitting 2: play together once through, notice any place the beat slipped apart
Sitting 3: fix that one spot slowly, then play together again
Sitting 4: play together once through as if recording
An old piece played together with the same family member or recording

steps.title: Record this week's version
steps.prompt: Record the duet in one take: say both names or say it is with a recording, then play together, hands in the frame.

extras.title: Make your own duet
extras.body:
Turn one of your solo pieces into a piece for two people.

Start with a question: what would this piece sound like as two parts played together instead of one?

Three constraints: use notes from the piece, play the second part's melody in half time, and land both parts on the beat.

Sketch first: write out the second part's notes before you try to play them.

You know it works when two people can play both parts together without stopping.
